subject: Agriculture
title: Rodents and Birds
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Rodents and Birds.

hook.text: Rats eat or contaminate 20% of the world's stored grain. In some regions, they rival insects as pests.

buildup.text: A pair of rats can produce 15,000 descendants in a year. Grain stores are rat paradise.

discovery.text: Quelea birds in Africa form flocks of 10 million that devour grain fields in minutes.

twist.text: Attempts to control quelea with aerial pesticide spraying killed millions of non-target birds and pollinators.

climax.text: Better storage infrastructure—metal silos instead of open bags—is more effective against rats than poison.

punchline.text: The biggest crop losses aren't in the field. They're in the warehouse.

quiz.question: What percentage of stored grain do rats eat or contaminate globally?

details.summary: Rodents and birds are among the oldest agricultural pests, causing billions of dollars in crop losses annually by consuming grain in the field and in storage. This topic covers the major species involved, their impact, and the methods farmers use to deter them.
details.whyItMatters: Rodents alone destroy enough grain to feed 200 million people each year. In Southeast Asia, rats cause up to 20% of rice losses. Managing these vertebrate pests requires different strategies than insect control.
takeaways: Rats destroy enough stored grain annually to feed 200 million people worldwide
Birds like quelea in Africa can devastate entire fields of grain in hours
Control methods include trapping, habitat management, scare devices, and exclusion

faq.question: Which rodents and birds cause the most agricultural damage?
faq.answer: The rice-field rat causes massive losses across Southeast Asia. The house mouse damages grain stores worldwide. The red-billed quelea, a small African bird, forms flocks of millions that strip grain fields bare. Starlings and parakeets damage fruit and grain crops globally.

faq.question: How do farmers protect crops from rodents and birds?
faq.answer: For rodents, farmers use trapping, bait stations, and barn owl nest boxes for biological control. For birds, strategies include netting, reflective tape, sound deterrents, and timing harvests to avoid peak bird activity. Integrated approaches work better than single methods.
